subtype: Rising pitch for questions and doubt [Interpreting]
passage: In the Delhi flat, Parveen practised her reading for the class quiz while her brother Ujjwal sat nearby with his cricket cards. She read, “The river is very long?” with her voice going up at the end. Ujjwal frowned. “Are you not sure?” She shook her head, surprised. “No, I am sure. I just say it like that when I'm being polite.” Ujjwal laughed. “Then everyone will think you don't know.” She tried again with her voice going down on “long,” and it sounded firm. “Oh, so it can be either,” he said, “you have to look at the rest of her face too.”

qa.q: What was Parveen practising for?
qa.a: The class quiz.

qa.q: Why did Ujjwal think Parveen was unsure?
qa.a: Her voice went up at the end of the sentence like a question, which he read as doubt, though she said it was her polite way of speaking.

qa.q: What could Ujjwal do next time he hears a rising voice?
qa.a: He could ask whether she is unsure and look at the rest of the situation before deciding it means doubt.

qa.q: How might Parveen's teacher hear the rising voice in the quiz?
qa.a: The teacher could take it for doubt and mark her as unsure, even if Parveen knows the answer.

grounding: A rising pitch may signal a question or uncertainty, but Parveen shows it can also be politeness, so context matters.

subtype: Rising pitch for questions and doubt [Interpreting]
passage: “Say it again, Kalyani,” said Arnab, tapping the table. “Ten past five?” Her voice climbed on the last word. “Are you asking me or telling me?” he said. “Telling you, silly!” Kalyani said, tilting her head. “In our village everyone talks that way. It goes up when we're being nice.” Arnab thought about it. “In my class if it goes up, the teacher says you're guessing.” “Well, I'm not guessing.” She said it again, falling on “five.” “See? Ten past five. Same words.” Arnab grinned. “Fine. Next time I'll ask before I decide you're unsure.”

qa.q: What time did Kalyani say?
qa.a: Ten past five.

qa.q: Why did Arnab ask if Kalyani was asking or telling?
qa.a: He heard her voice rise on the last word and wondered if she was unsure, since his teacher treats a rising voice as guessing.

qa.q: What did Arnab decide to do differently?
qa.a: He decided to ask before assuming Kalyani is unsure, because a rising voice can be a regional habit and not doubt.

qa.q: How might Kalyani feel when her friends read her habit as guessing?
qa.a: She might feel misunderstood or annoyed, since to her the rising voice is just politeness from home. 😅

grounding: A rising tone can mean a question or doubt, but for Kalyani it is politeness and a regional habit.

passage: Last week I had a cold, and my voice came out nasal and rough. When I answered in class, Nandini copied me in a silly voice and some kids laughed. My face went hot. I wanted to say, “It's my cold!” but nothing came. That evening Mummy gave me warm water and said the voice was because my nose was blocked and my throat was sore. It was my body, not my mood. Next day I told Nandini, “I'm not sad or grumpy, I'm just sick.” She looked ashamed and said sorry. I'm Farida, and I understand my voice a bit better now.

qa.q: What did Nandini do when Farida answered in class?
qa.a: She copied Farida in a silly voice.

qa.q: How did Farida feel when the class laughed, and how do you know?
qa.a: Farida felt embarrassed, since Farida's face went hot and words to explain would not come.

qa.q: What did Farida do that helped clear things up?
qa.a: Farida told Nandini it was a cold, not sadness or grumpiness, which explained the voice.

qa.q: Why might Nandini have misread Farida's voice?
qa.a: Nandini may have thought the strange voice meant a mood or was just funny, without thinking it came from a cold.

grounding: A nasal, raspy voice reflects a cold and body state, not mood, and mocking it is a misreading.

passage: Counsellor's note, Class 5. Dilnaz came to see me because some classmates called her voice “angry crow.” Her voice has been raspy for four days after cheering at the sports day. She wondered aloud if she sounded mean. I explained that a raspy voice usually tells us something about the throat, not the feelings, and that a doctor could look if it keeps going or worries her. With her permission, I spoke to Maria, who had joined in the teasing. Maria said she had assumed Dilnaz was grumpy. She agreed to apologise. Dilnaz drank water and left smiling a little. Ms. Maria's class will hear a short talk on voices. Counsellor.

qa.q: How long has Dilnaz's voice been raspy?
qa.a: Four days.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz worried about when she came to the counsellor?
qa.a: She wondered whether her raspy voice made her sound mean to others.

qa.q: What could Dilnaz do if the raspy voice keeps going?
qa.a: She could tell a trusted adult and check with the doctor if it keeps going or worries her.

qa.q: Why might Maria have joined in the teasing?
qa.a: Maria assumed Dilnaz was grumpy because of how she sounded, so she read a body state as a mood.

grounding: A raspy voice from shouting reflects body state, peers misread it as mood, and an adult teaches that voice quality is body first.

passage: Mr. Joseph asked the Class 6 group to read their poems aloud. When Jomon's turn came, his voice went tight and thin, and he stopped mid-line to swallow. His eyes were shiny. Avni, who sat beside him, stared. Was he being rude by not looking up? The teacher walked over calmly. “Take a slow breath, Jomon. Here is some water.” Jomon breathed in slowly and sipped. Mr. Joseph said, “Take your time, we can wait.” Jomon's voice loosened a little as he read the next line. Avni looked down at her own poem and smiled. She thought he was trying very hard.

qa.q: What did Mr. Joseph give Jomon?
qa.a: Some water.

qa.q: What might Jomon have been feeling when his voice went tight and thin?
qa.a: He was probably nervous or close to tears about reading in front of the group, and the strain shows how hard he was trying to cope.

qa.q: What helped loosen Jomon's voice?
qa.a: Slow breathing and a sip of water, together with the teacher's patience.

qa.q: How did Avni's view of Jomon change?
qa.a: She first wondered if he was being rude, then saw him as someone trying very hard.

grounding: A child holds back emotion with a strained voice, slow breathing and water help, and an adult reads strain as coping.

passage: I saw it in the school corridor. Saurabh had just been told that his football was not returned, and when Chetan asked what happened, Saurabh answered in a really tight voice, like every word was being squeezed out. His hands were shut into fists. I thought he might be angry with Chetan, but then Saurabh bit his lip and turned aside, and I saw his eyes were wet. Chetan just stood next to him and said nothing. After a moment, Saurabh took a deep breath and said, in a softer voice, “I'm just upset about the ball.” I am not sure he was only upset. He might have been scared too.

qa.q: What had happened to Saurabh's football?
qa.a: It was not returned.

qa.q: What did the observer think Saurabh might be feeling, and what else could it be?
qa.a: The observer first thought he was angry, then thought he was upset and holding back tears, and also wondered if he was scared.

qa.q: What helped Saurabh's voice soften?
qa.a: Chetan stood quietly beside him without pressing, and Saurabh took a deep breath.

qa.q: How might Chetan have felt hearing that tight voice?
qa.a: He might have felt unsure or worried he had caused it, so quiet company was a kind choice.

grounding: A child holding back tears or anger speaks in a strained voice, which is effort to cope, not defiance.

passage: Kofi came home from school in Accra and dropped his bag by the door. “How was the test?” his older sister Dalia asked. “Fine.” “Did you eat lunch?” “Yes.” “Was Yaw there?” “No.” Each answer was short and flat, and he headed straight for his room. Dalia opened her mouth to ask more, then stopped. She thought he might be tired, or hurt about something, or just not ready. Instead she made two cups of hot chocolate, set one outside his door, and said, “I'm on the balcony if you want to talk.” Half an hour later, Kofi came out and sat down beside her.

qa.q: Where did Dalia sit after leaving the cup outside Kofi's door?
qa.a: On the balcony.

qa.q: What did Dalia think Kofi's short answers might mean?
qa.a: She thought he might be tired, hurt about something or not ready to talk yet.

qa.q: Why was Dalia's plan better than asking more questions?
qa.a: It gave him time and a low-pressure moment, so he could come to her when he was ready.

qa.q: How might Kofi have felt about being asked so many questions right after school?
qa.a: He may have felt tired and wanted a quiet moment, so the questions could have felt like pressure.

grounding: Clipped replies after a hard day may mean tiredness, hurt or unreadiness, and offering time works better than demanding detail.

passage: After the afternoon bell, Akash walked into the school counselling room and dropped into a chair. Ms. Aparna asked, “How did the match go?” “Okay.” “Did you play well?” “Yeah.” “And your friends?” “Fine.” His replies were short, and he looked at the wall. She waited and then said, “You don't have to tell me now. I have some crayons and paper if you'd like to draw, and I'll be here till four.” Akash shrugged, but pulled the crayons over. Ten minutes later, without looking up, he said, “Ravi didn't pass me the ball all day.” Ms. Aparna nodded.

qa.q: How long did Ms. Aparna say she would be there?
qa.a: Until four.

qa.q: What might Akash have been feeling when he gave clipped answers?
qa.a: He may have felt hurt about the match and not ready to talk, which explains why he only shared later about the ball.

qa.q: What did Ms. Aparna do that made it easier for Akash to share?
qa.a: She stopped pushing for detail and offered crayons and time, so he could talk when he was ready.

qa.q: How might Ravi's behaviour look to Akash, compared with how Ravi might see it?
qa.a: Akash felt left out of the game, while Ravi may not have realised his passing left Akash hurt.

grounding: A child with clipped answers after a hard match may be hurt or unready to talk, and the counsellor offers time.

passage: Thursday. Today Mrs. Dutta asked us who wanted to present the science project, and I stood up so fast my chair fell. “I. Have. Worked. On. This. For. Two. Weeks,” I said, slowly, pressing every word. The class went quiet. I wasn't angry, I wanted them to know how much it meant to me. Amandeep thought I was cross and whispered, “Chill.” But Mrs. Dutta smiled and said, “I can see how much this matters to you.” I felt proud. I hope that next time I can say it in a way people don't mistake for shouting. Chandrika.

qa.q: How long had Chandrika worked on the project?
qa.a: Two weeks.

qa.q: Why did Chandrika stress every word and speak slowly?
qa.a: Chandrika wanted the class to know how much the project mattered and felt proud of the work.

qa.q: What could Chandrika try next time so people do not mistake her emphasis for anger?
qa.a: Chandrika could smile or say “this is really important to me” along with the slow words.

qa.q: How did Amandeep read Chandrika's voice?
qa.a: Amandeep thought Chandrika was cross and whispered “Chill,” which shows how emphasis can be misread as rudeness.

grounding: Emphatic, slow speech can show importance or pride, and adults read it as what matters most to the child.

passage: Chinmay stood at the front of the small classroom in Maddur, gripping his drawing of the tractor. “This is my grandfather's tractor,” he said, pausing on each word. “It is the BIGGEST in our village, and it started before anyone else's.” He stressed “biggest” and lifted his chin. Some of the boys smirked. Eshaan whispered, “He's showing off.” But the teacher, Mr. Reddy, noticed how Chinmay held the paper and how slowly he spoke. “You are proud of it,” Mr. Reddy said. Chinmay nodded quickly. “Yes, sir! He taught me to drive it in the field.” His voice grew softer and his shoulders dropped.

qa.q: Whose tractor was Chinmay's drawing of?
qa.a: His grandfather's.

qa.q: What was Chinmay feeling when he stressed the word biggest?
qa.a: He felt proud of his grandfather's tractor, and his lifted chin and slow words showed it.

qa.q: How could Eshaan understand Chinmay better?
qa.a: He could ask about the tractor and listen to why it matters, not decide it is showing off.

qa.q: Why might Eshaan and Mr. Reddy read the same emphasis differently?
qa.a: Eshaan may hear boasting, while Mr. Reddy watched how Chinmay held his paper and heard pride.

grounding: Emphatic speech with stress and slow pace shows what matters to a child, and can be pride, not rudeness.

passage: In the Chennai apartment corridor, a flower pot lay broken. Vikas's mother was not home, and his cousin Deepak stood next to him. When Vikas's aunt asked, “Who broke it?”, Deepak paused, his eyes on the tiles. The pause was long. Vikas's stomach tightened. His aunt did not shout. She said quietly, “I'm not angry. I just want to know what happened.” Deepak breathed out. “The ball hit it. It was me. Vikas said he'd tell you, but I wanted to.” His aunt nodded. “Thank you for telling me.” Vikas realised Deepak's pause had been fear, not a lie.

qa.q: What was broken in the corridor?
qa.a: A flower pot.

qa.q: What did Deepak's long pause seem to be about?
qa.a: It seemed to come from fear of the consequences, since he answered honestly once his aunt said she was not angry.

qa.q: What did the aunt do that helped Deepak tell the truth?
qa.a: She stayed calm and said she only wanted to know what happened, instead of accusing him.

qa.q: How might Vikas have felt while watching the pause?
qa.a: He was tense, perhaps worried for his cousin or that he would be blamed, and afterward he understood the pause was fear, not lying.

grounding: A hesitation before answering can be fear of consequences, not proof of lying, and a calm follow-up brings honesty.

passage: “Well?” said Deepika's mother, holding the empty biscuit tin. “Did you take them?” Deepika looked at her shoes. “Um... I...” The pause stretched. Farida, her friend, sitting on the sofa, quickly said, “Aunty, we shared them.” “Deepika, look at me,” said her mother in a sharp voice, and Deepika's shoulders went up. Then her mother sighed and lowered her voice. “Take your time. I'm not shouting.” Deepika swallowed. “I had two, and Farida had two. The rest I gave to the neighbour's dog. I was scared you'd be cross about the dog.” Her mother almost laughed. “Next time just tell me.”

qa.q: How many biscuits did Deepika have?
qa.a: Two.

qa.q: What was Deepika afraid of when she hesitated?
qa.a: She was afraid her mother would be cross about giving biscuits to the neighbour's dog, so she hesitated before answering.

qa.q: What made Deepika able to tell the truth?
qa.a: Her mother lowered her voice and said she was not shouting and Deepika could take her time.

qa.q: How might Deepika's mother have read the first long pause?
qa.a: She may have taken it as a sign Deepika was hiding something, though it turned out she was just nervous about the dog.

grounding: Hesitation can mean worry about consequences and is not proof of lying, and calm follow-up works better than accusation.

passage:
Monday. In Miss Ankita's class, Francis shouted an answer before she finished the question. Miss Ankita said gently, “Raise your hand, Francis.”

Wednesday. Francis remembered. He put up his hand, though it took great effort to keep the answer in his mouth. Miss Ankita nodded at him. “Yes, Francis?” His answer was right, and he grinned.

Saturday. At his cousin's wedding, everyone talked over each other at dinner, and Francis was told to join in. He waited for a pause but it never came, so he began talking too, and Uncle laughed. Francis noticed that at home overlapping talk showed everyone was interested.

qa.q: On which day did Francis raise his hand and wait?
qa.a: On Wednesday.

qa.q: What did Francis feel when he kept his answer in his mouth on Wednesday?
qa.a: It took great effort, so he was probably impatient and eager to answer, but he held back.

qa.q: What did Francis learn about interruptions across the three days?
qa.a: He learned that classrooms ask for raised hands and waiting, while at the family dinner overlapping talk showed interest.

qa.q: How might Uncle have seen Francis joining in at dinner?
qa.a: Uncle laughed, so he probably took it as warm, lively interest in the conversation.

grounding: A child learns to raise a hand and wait at school, while overlapping talk in the family shows warmth, so norms vary.

passage: Manjula, you ask why I let you talk over me at the table but tell you to wait in school. Let me tell you a story. When I was ten, our teacher, Devika Ma'am, had a rule: one person speaks, the rest listen. At home, though, my aunts and my grandmother talked all at once and finished each other's sentences, and nobody minded. I once waited at the dinner table for a gap to speak, and my grandmother asked, “Why so quiet? Are you unwell?” So I learned there are two ways. The classroom asks you to wait. My grandmother's table welcomed the noise.

qa.q: How old was the storyteller when Devika Ma'am set her rule?
qa.a: Ten.

qa.q: Why did the grandmother ask if the child was unwell at the dinner table?
qa.a: She read the waiting and silence as something wrong, since in her family talking together showed interest.

qa.q: What should a child remember when moving between school and home?
qa.a: Different places have different rules about interrupting, so the child can follow the rule of the place.

qa.q: How might Devika Ma'am see the overlapping talk at the aunts' dinner table?
qa.a: She might find it unusual or noisy for a classroom, but at home she could see it as a sign of closeness.

grounding: Interruption norms vary by setting, so overlapping talk shows warmth in some families and seems disrespectful in a classroom.

passage:
Monday. Pradeep stood at the back of assembly with his lips shut while the other children sang the prayer song. He looked at the ground.

Wednesday. Chaitanya, standing next to him, quietly began to hum. Pradeep hummed too, very softly. The teacher, Mr. Gopal, smiled from the front and said nothing.

Friday. The whole school chanted the sports-day cheer, and Pradeep found himself shouting with everyone. Afterwards his cheeks were red and he was grinning. “I liked that one,” he told Chaitanya. “The other songs feel too big and everyone can hear me, but here I'm one of the many.”

qa.q: Who began to hum on Wednesday?
qa.a: Chaitanya.

qa.q: Why did Pradeep stay quiet on Monday?
qa.a: He seemed shy about being heard in front of the others, not disrespectful, as he later said the other songs feel too big and everyone can hear him.

qa.q: What helped Pradeep join in?
qa.a: Chaitanya humming next to him and the sports-day cheer, where he felt like one of many.

qa.q: How might Mr. Gopal have seen Pradeep's silence on Monday?
qa.a: He might have noticed it and wondered about shyness, and his smile on Wednesday shows he accepted the soft humming.

grounding: Group chanting can lift mood and belonging, and a child who does not sing may be shy rather than disrespectful.

passage: Sabina, when you complain about singing at assembly, I remember something from when I was twelve, in Coimbatore. Every Friday our class chanted the bhajan in the hall, and I hated my voice. I stood at the back and just moved my lips. The teacher never scolded me. One day, Karthik, my friend, stood beside me and sang loudly and out of tune. I laughed so hard that I forgot to be shy and I joined in. That day I felt part of something bigger than me. It's fine if you're not ready, child. But when you sing with others, your voice doesn't have to be perfect. It just has to be there.

qa.q: Where did the bhajan take place every Friday?
qa.a: In the hall, with the class.

qa.q: Why did the storyteller only move the lips at first?
qa.a: The storyteller disliked singing aloud and felt shy, not disrespectful, so stood at the back and mouthed the words.

qa.q: What helped the storyteller start singing?
qa.a: Karthik stood beside the storyteller and sang loudly and out of tune, which brought laughter and made the shyness fade.

qa.q: How might the teacher have seen the child who only moved the lips?
qa.a: The teacher did not scold, so probably understood it as shyness and let the child join when ready.

grounding: Group singing brings belonging, and a child who does not sing may be shy, which an elder recalls from his own school days.

subtype: Vocal imitation as humour or mockery [Mismatch]
passage: On the school bus in Mumbai, Pranav began copying the driver's habit of saying, “Sit, sit, sit down now,” in a deep, comic voice. Vidya, next to him, giggled. Then Pranav did the same to the conductor, who was walking down the aisle, and the conductor turned around slowly. Pranav stopped. Vidya stopped smiling, too. The conductor said nothing. He just looked, then smiled a little and shook his head. Vidya whispered, “That was a bit much.” Pranav's ears were hot. “I was only playing,” he said. “Maybe check if he's laughing first,” said Vidya.

qa.q: Whose voice did Pranav copy first?
qa.a: The driver's.

qa.q: Why did Pranav say he was only playing, and what else might his hot ears suggest?
qa.a: He meant it as fun, but hot ears suggest he also felt embarrassed once the conductor turned around.

qa.q: What could Pranav try next time he wants to imitate someone?
qa.a: He could look to see whether the other person is laughing too, as Vidya suggested, before continuing.

qa.q: How might the conductor have felt about being imitated?
qa.a: He might have felt mocked or he might have taken it lightly, and his slow turn and small smile leave it unclear.

grounding: A child's imitation of a voice can be play or mockery, and the target's reaction decides.

subtype: Vocal imitation as humour or mockery [Mismatch]
passage: “Hello, class, sit down,” boomed Indu in her deepest voice, hands on hips, and Payal fell off the sofa laughing. “Again! Do Mrs. Nair!” Indu did, with a wobble on the r's. Payal was crying with laughter. “Do Mummy now!” “No,” said Indu, and stopped. “Why not?” “Mummy said the last time I did her, she felt I was making fun.” Payal frowned. “But I like it.” “You laugh, but Mummy didn't.” Payal thought. “Then let's do only the ones who laugh with us,” she said. Indu nodded and did the cook, who chuckled from the kitchen.

qa.q: Whose voice did Indu imitate that made Payal laugh so hard?
qa.a: Mrs. Nair's.

qa.q: Why did Indu refuse to imitate Mummy?
qa.a: She remembered that Mummy felt she was being mocked the last time, so Indu did not want to hurt her.

qa.q: What rule did the girls come up with, and why is it useful?
qa.a: They chose to imitate only people who laugh along, which shows whether it is kind play or unkind mimicry.

qa.q: How might Mummy have felt about the imitation?
qa.a: She probably felt hurt or teased, since she did not laugh, even though Payal thought it was funny. 🙂

grounding: Imitating a voice can be affectionate play or unkind mockery, and the target's reaction decides.

passage: During Class 6 morning break, I watched Deepak wave at Mahima as she crossed the corridor. She kept walking, head down, holding her books. Deepak's hand fell. He sat down heavily on the bench and said to me, “She didn't even look.” I didn't know what to say. Later, I saw Mahima at the water stand with her eyes red, maybe because of a headache or worry about the test. I don't know. When she came back, Deepak said, “Hi,” and she smiled and answered. Deepak grinned and looked embarrassed at once. “I guess she just didn't see me,” he told me.

qa.q: Who waved at Mahima in the corridor?
qa.a: Deepak.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel when Mahima did not respond to his wave, and what did he later conclude?
qa.a: He felt hurt and snubbed, but after she smiled and replied later, he thought she might simply not have seen him.

qa.q: What could Deepak do next time someone ignores his hello?
qa.a: He could check again later, as he did, before deciding it means unfriendliness.

qa.q: How might Mahima have been feeling when she passed the corridor?
qa.a: She may have been worried or unwell, since her eyes were red later, so she was probably busy with her own thoughts.

grounding: A missed hello may be inattention rather than snub, and checking twice before feeling hurt is wise.

passage:
Monday. Avni gave a big smile to the new boy Jomon at the gate, but he looked past her. Avni went quiet all morning, thinking he didn't like her.

Wednesday. She said hello again in the corridor. Jomon jumped, took out earphones and said, “Oh, sorry, I was listening to a story!” Avni laughed, a bit surprised.

Friday. Jomon waved to her from far away at the canteen, and Avni waved back. “I thought you ignored me,” she told him. “I did not see you on Monday,” he said. “I'm still learning where everyone is.”

qa.q: What was Jomon doing on Wednesday when Avni said hello again?
qa.a: He was listening to a story with earphones.

qa.q: What did Avni first think when Jomon looked past her at the gate?
qa.a: She thought he did not like her and felt hurt, so she stayed quiet all morning.

qa.q: What did Avni do that helped her read the situation better?
qa.a: She said hello again on Wednesday instead of deciding on Monday that he was cold.

qa.q: How might Jomon have felt as a new boy on the first days?
qa.a: He was probably busy learning where everyone is, so he missed the smile without meaning to be unfriendly. 🙂

grounding: A missed hello may be inattention, and a child checks twice before feeling hurt.
